title: 2.3.27 switch or if...else? Justify Your Choice
description: Explain which statement fits a given problem and why. AI-graded.
sourceRef: book 2.3.6: Concepts in Practice: Picking the right tool; why the grade chain can't become a switch

aiGrader.rubricTitle: switch or if...else? Justify Your Choice: AI-graded rubric
aiGrader.prompt:
Answer all three, numbered Q1 to Q3. Everything you need is in 2.3.23 (Choosing Between if...else and switch) and the worked examples in 2.3.24 and 2.3.25: go back and reread them if you get stuck. A few sentences each is plenty, in your own everyday words.

Q1: A program routes a support ticket by its priority, which is always one of 'low', 'medium', or 'high'. Which statement fits better, switch or if...else? Explain why, in terms of what is being compared. (2.3.23, and the worked example in 2.3.24)

Q2: The grade chain from this section (score >= 90 prints A, score >= 80 prints B, and so on) cannot be rewritten as a switch. Explain why, in your own words. (2.3.23, and the worked example in 2.3.25)

Q3: Describe one program of your own choosing, real or made up, that could use either a switch or an if...else chain. Say which one you would pick and how you decided, using the same test from the reading. (2.3.23)

rubric.title: Q1: Picks switch and explains why
rubric.description: Answer picks switch and explains that priority is a single value compared against a fixed, finite list of exact strings ('low', 'medium', 'high') with no ranges involved. Deny if the answer picks if...else, or picks switch without explaining the finite-list reasoning.

rubric.title: Q2: Explains why the grade chain can't become a switch
rubric.description: Answer explains that score >= 80 (and similar) is a range covering many values, not one exact value, so there is no finite list of case values that could represent it. Accept any phrasing that identifies the range/boundary nature of the condition as the blocker. Deny an answer that only says 'switch doesn't support >=' without explaining why that matters (the finite-list requirement).

rubric.title: Q3: Gives an own-choice example with a justified pick
rubric.description: Describes a concrete program scenario (not the priority or grade example already used), states which statement it would use, and justifies the pick by asking whether the test can be written as a finite list of exact values. Deny if no reasoning is given for the choice, or if the example is just restated from Q1/Q2.
